When a circle $\odot P$ with radius $4$ is tangent to one side of $\triangle ABC$, what is the length of $CP$?
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:

Given that in right triangle $ABC$, $AC=5$, $BC=12$,\\
therefore $AB=\sqrt{AC^2+BC^2}=\sqrt{5^2+12^2}=13$,\\
since $CD\perp AB$,\\
the area of $\triangle ABC = \frac{1}{2}AB\cdot CD=\frac{1}{2}AC\cdot BC$,\\
thus, $13CD=5\times 12$,\\
therefore, $CD= \frac{60}{13}$,\\
considering three cases:\\
(1) When circle $P$ is tangent to side $BC$, as shown in the figure:\\
Draw $PE\perp BC$ at point E,\\
since $PE \perp BC$,\\
thus $\angle PEC=90^\circ$,\\
hence $\angle PCE+\angle CPE=90^\circ$, and $\angle PCE+\angle B=90^\circ$,\\
therefore, $\angle B=\angle CPE$,\\
since $\angle CEP=\angle ACB=90^\circ$,\\
thus $\triangle BCA\sim \triangle PEC$,\\
hence $\frac{BA}{PC}=\frac{BC}{PE}$,\\
therefore, $\frac{13}{PC}=\frac{12}{4}$,\\
thus, $PC=\frac{13}{3}$,\\
(2) When circle $P$ is tangent to side $AB$, as shown in the figure:\\
since $PD\perp AB$,\\
therefore, $CP=CD-PD=\frac{60}{13}-4=\frac{8}{13}$,\\
(3) When circle $P$ is tangent to side $AC$, as shown in the figure:\\
Draw $PF\perp AC$ at point F,\\
since $PF\perp AC$,\\
thus $\angle PFC=90^\circ$,\\
hence $\angle CPF+\angle PCF=90^\circ$, and $\angle A+\angle PCF=90^\circ$\\
therefore, $\angle A=\angle CPF$,\\
since $\angle CFP=\angle ACB=90^\circ$,\\
thus $\triangle BCA\sim \triangle CFP$,\\
hence $\frac{BA}{PC}=\frac{CA}{FP}$,\\
therefore, $\frac{13}{PC}=\frac{5}{4}$,\\
thus, $PC=\frac{52}{5}$,\\
since $\frac{52}{5}>\frac{60}{13}$\\
therefore, $PC=\frac{52}{5}$ (discarded)\\
In conclusion, when circle $P$ with radius 4 is tangent to one side of $\triangle ABC$, the length of $CP$ could be: $\boxed{\frac{13}{3}}$ or $\frac{8}{13}$.

When a circle $\odot P$ with radius $4$ is tangent to one side of $\triangle ABC$, what is the length of $CP$?
raw_record.answer:
\textbf{Solution:}

Given that in right triangle $ABC$, $AC=5$, $BC=12$,\\
therefore $AB=\sqrt{AC^2+BC^2}=\sqrt{5^2+12^2}=13$,\\
since $CD\perp AB$,\\
the area of $\triangle ABC = \frac{1}{2}AB\cdot CD=\frac{1}{2}AC\cdot BC$,\\
thus, $13CD=5\times 12$,\\
therefore, $CD= \frac{60}{13}$,\\
considering three cases:\\
(1) When circle $P$ is tangent to side $BC$, as shown in the figure:\\
Draw $PE\perp BC$ at point E,\\
since $PE \perp BC$,\\
thus $\angle PEC=90^\circ$,\\
hence $\angle PCE+\angle CPE=90^\circ$, and $\angle PCE+\angle B=90^\circ$,\\
therefore, $\angle B=\angle CPE$,\\
since $\angle CEP=\angle ACB=90^\circ$,\\
thus $\triangle BCA\sim \triangle PEC$,\\
hence $\frac{BA}{PC}=\frac{BC}{PE}$,\\
therefore, $\frac{13}{PC}=\frac{12}{4}$,\\
thus, $PC=\frac{13}{3}$,\\
(2) When circle $P$ is tangent to side $AB$, as shown in the figure:\\
since $PD\perp AB$,\\
therefore, $CP=CD-PD=\frac{60}{13}-4=\frac{8}{13}$,\\
(3) When circle $P$ is tangent to side $AC$, as shown in the figure:\\
Draw $PF\perp AC$ at point F,\\
since $PF\perp AC$,\\
thus $\angle PFC=90^\circ$,\\
hence $\angle CPF+\angle PCF=90^\circ$, and $\angle A+\angle PCF=90^\circ$\\
therefore, $\angle A=\angle CPF$,\\
since $\angle CFP=\angle ACB=90^\circ$,\\
thus $\triangle BCA\sim \triangle CFP$,\\
hence $\frac{BA}{PC}=\frac{CA}{FP}$,\\
therefore, $\frac{13}{PC}=\frac{5}{4}$,\\
thus, $PC=\frac{52}{5}$,\\
since $\frac{52}{5}>\frac{60}{13}$\\
therefore, $PC=\frac{52}{5}$ (discarded)\\
In conclusion, when circle $P$ with radius 4 is tangent to one side of $\triangle ABC$, the length of $CP$ could be: $\boxed{\frac{13}{3}}$ or $\frac{8}{13}$
